text: Almost every superconducting quantum computer you've heard of — IBM's, Google's, Rigetti's — runs on some variant of one design: the transmon. This lesson is about what makes it different, and why it became the default.

Before the transmon, one of the main designs was the charge qubit, or Cooper-pair box: a small superconducting island connected through a Josephson junction, where zero and one correspond to different numbers of extra Cooper pairs sitting on that island. The problem is charge noise — tiny, uncontrolled fluctuations in stray electric charge on the chip directly shift the qubit's energy levels and degrade coherence. The transmon's fix is a large capacitor wired in parallel with the junction. That shunting capacitor flattens out how sensitive the qubit's energy levels are to the exact charge on the island, which washes out the sharp charge-sensitivity that plagued the original design.

Here's what one of these chips actually looks like once it's fabricated and packaged — mounted between gold-plated microwave connector blocks that carry the control and readout lines. This whole assembly is what gets lowered down through the dilution refrigerator's stages to the coldest plate.

That fix isn't free. The same shunting capacitor that suppresses charge noise also reduces the circuit's anharmonicity — the gap between the zero-to-one and one-to-two transitions. A transmon's anharmonicity typically lands at just a few hundred megahertz, a much smaller gap to work with when designing fast control pulses that need to avoid accidentally driving the second excited state. More shunting capacitance buys better noise immunity but leaves less separation to control against.

Good charge-noise immunity, manufacturable with well-understood fabrication, and anharmonicity that's still workable — that combination is why IBM, Google, and Rigetti all build around transmon-family qubits today, even though their fabrication, connectivity, and control electronics differ. Next lesson: the two numbers that describe how long a qubit actually holds onto its quantum information — T1 and T2.
